item.title: OpenAI lets AI agents make purchases using tokenized payments
item.description:
Source: Engadget, TechCrunch, The Verge, Gizmodo, Digital Trends Original headline: OpenAI Launches ChatGPT Wallet, Allowing AI Agents to Make Purchases on Users' Behalf
OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet, allowing AI agents to make purchases using payment tokens instead of sharing card details. Users input payment info once, generating tokens for transactions, which require biometric approval. The feature is available to U.S. ChatGPT Pro subscribers aged 18+ with American Express, Mastercard, or Visa. OpenAI claims users retain credit card rewards and protections. Partnerships with payment networks aim to secure transactions, though Amazon and others have banned AI agents. Future updates may include spending limits and pre-approved purchases. Privacy concerns arise from detailed purchase records, though OpenAI states it won’t sell data. While AI shopping tools like Meta’s Muse see usage, companies like Uber and DoorDash report low AI-driven orders. Public skepticism remains, with 77% concerned about AI handling financial transactions. The system avoids sharing actual card details, using tokenization for security. Challenges include retailer bans and regulatory hurdles as OpenAI refines the feature for broader adoption.
item.source: Engadget, TechCrunch, The Verge, Gizmodo, Digital Trends

item.title: Nuclear Tests Left Lingering Carbon-14 in Canadian Maple Trees for 60 Years
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Original headline: Nuclear Tests Left Something Behind in Canada’s Iconic Maples—and It Lasted 60 Years
Nuclear tests during the Cold War left a lasting carbon-14 signature in Canada’s sugar maple trees. The bomb pulse, caused by above-ground nuclear tests, doubled atmospheric carbon-14 levels. In Gatineau Park, maple leaves reached peak bomb-pulse carbon-14 levels of 842 parts per thousand in 1964, but levels remained elevated for 60 years, dropping to -13.9 parts per thousand by 2025. Researchers at the University of Ottawa found that trees absorb older carbon from previous years, delaying their radiocarbon response. This delayed absorption, confirmed by data from 1990-2019, means tree-based atmospheric reconstructions must account for species-specific delays. Fossil fuel use since the 1960s diluted the carbon-14, overwhelming bomb-pulse residuals by 2025. The study, published in Scientific Reports, highlights how trees act as long-term recorders of atmospheric changes, with oceans also absorbing excess carbon-14. The findings challenge previous assumptions about the immediacy of plant-atmosphere carbon-14 correlations.

item.title: Google lets Gemini connect to bank accounts for financial analysis
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: Google now lets people connect Gemini to their bank accounts
Google allows Gemini users to connect the chatbot to their bank accounts via Google Wallet for financial analysis. The integration focuses on spending insights rather than transactional capabilities, enabling users to identify subscription price changes and create budgets with dynamic charts. Security measures include restrictions preventing Gemini from moving or managing funds, with the feature being opt-in and adjustable via settings. Google partnered with fintech firm Plaid to provide deeper financial insights, though details remain unspecified. The move follows trends of AI chatbots accessing financial data, including OpenAI's Dots agents and Meta's Muse, which have faced bans from companies like United Airlines and Amazon over shopping automation concerns.

item.title: Scientists Identify Age-Related Cold Sensitivity Cause in Brown Fat Cells
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Original headline: Scientists Figured Out Why We Feel Colder as We Age—and It’s Not What You Think
Scientists at City of Hope Medical Center discovered that aging reduces the ability of brown fat cells to generate heat, explaining why older people feel colder. Using mice models, researchers found that certain immune cells produce proteins that keep brown fat cells in an inactive state. In older mice, these proteins remained elevated, preventing effective heat production. A drug called mifepristone, used to block the proteins' effects, reversed some age-related slowdown in brown fat activity. While the findings suggest potential treatments for age-related metabolic issues like obesity and diabetes, the drug is not suitable for human use due to its broad effects. Senior author Qiong Wang noted that restoring brown fat function could address declining thermogenic activity with age. The study highlights a biological basis for cold sensitivity in older adults, offering new avenues for metabolic research.

item.title: Wine 11.22 adds AVX support for ARM64 Linux apps
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Original headline: Your x86 Windows apps may now run on ARM64 thanks to Wine's AVX support
Wine 11.22 adds AVX support for x86 applications on ARM64 Linux systems, improving compatibility. The update includes address space randomization, a security feature similar to Windows' ASLR, to make memory layouts less predictable. Linuxiac reported the addition of ASLR and other improvements like updated Unicode CLDR 49 locale data, enhanced Tahoma font metrics, and reimplementation of MSXML DTD validation. Bug fixes address issues in games such as Dragon Age: Origins, Black Mirror II/III, Guild Wars 2, Alan Wake, and F.E.A.R. 3. The Vulkan renderer was updated to resolve crashes and visual bugs. Other fixes include resolving a missing RGB565 Vulkan swapchain fallback, correcting Notepad++ menu bars, and fixing crashes in WinSCP, Logos Bible Software, and FreeCommander. System-level fixes address thread-handling, Windows Management Instrumentation properties, and ECDSA key support. Source code and binary packages are available for download.

item.title: LangChain hits $3B valuation with $300M Series C
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Original headline: AI agent startup LangChain hits $3B valuation
LangChain raised a $300 million Series C round at a $3 billion valuation, led by CapitalG. The funding includes participation from GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures. This more than doubles its previous $1.25 billion valuation following a $125 million round a year ago. Founded in 2022 as an open-source project, LangChain initially focused on tasks like web searching and API calls, which early LLMs struggled with. It now specializes in managing AI agents, emphasizing business ownership of intelligence through its LangSmith platform. LangSmith is designed to avoid vendor lock-in by supporting multiple models, clouds, and ecosystems. The company claims 7,000 customers, including Harvey, Rippling, Clay, Nvidia, Toyota, and Salesforce. While competitors like Mintive offer similar tools, LangChain’s early start and broad adoption position it as a leader in the space.

item.title: FAA Expands AI System to Manage National Airspace Congestion
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Original headline: FAA expands AI advice to manage air traffic congestion across entire US airspace
The FAA has expanded the use of its SMART AI system to manage air traffic across the entire US airspace. The $875 million system, initially tested in Washington, DC, rerouted 180 flights since September 21, saving an average of 10 minutes per flight and 80 gallons of fuel. The agency aims to replicate these results nationwide by deploying SMART in all 22 air traffic control centers. SMART, a cloud-based tool, combines data on weather, flight paths, traffic flow, and staffing to predict patterns and recommend optimal routes. Airline executives support the rollout, while the union representing air traffic controllers notes they were not involved in designing or testing the system. FAA specialists in DC validate SMART recommendations before they are sent to control facilities. The system is designed to reduce delays, fuel use, and improve travel experiences.

item.title: Steam Adds Real-World Frame Rates for Steam Deck Games
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Original headline: Will that game run like crap on your PC? Steam finally has some answers
Steam is adding real-world frame rate data for games on the Steam Deck, helping users gauge performance before purchasing. The platform now displays average frame rates and histograms showing performance distribution for thousands of games, collected from opt-in players. Verified, Playable, and Unsupported games are included, with examples like Cyberpunk 2077 (30-40 fps) and Skyrim: Special Edition (50-60 fps). The Steam Deck OLED now costs $789, up $240 from before, while the 1TB model hits $949, up $300. Valve aims to expand this data to other devices, seeking desktop beta users to contribute frame-rate info. The move addresses long-standing issues with generic system requirements and hardware variability, offering a potential solution for predicting PC game performance. Developers could gain insights into how games perform across diverse PC setups, though challenges remain with differing configurations like resolution and drivers.

item.title: Google Updates Search with Gemini 4 Hydrogen for Visual, Intent-Based Results
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Original headline: Visual flair—Google's Gemini 4 Hydrogen AI made Search a lot more casual
Google updated Search with Gemini 4 Hydrogen, enhancing visual responses and intent understanding. The AI model provides images, tables, and structured data for complex queries, such as restaurant recommendations with dietary restrictions. Gemini 4 Hydrogen improves back-linking, helping users find information from new sources. Search now prioritizes prominent source links, making verification easier. Google also introduced engaging thumbnails and a carousel of news articles for breaking news. The update builds on previous AI Mode features, offering a more intuitive search experience. Users can access Hydrogen via the plus icon in AI Mode, with it set as the default model. The changes aim to simplify information retrieval and improve search accuracy through advanced AI capabilities.

item.title: ElevenLabs Introduces ElevenAI for Team Meeting Productivity
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch, Digital Trends Original headline: ElevenLabs Launches ElevenAI to Revolutionize Team Meeting Productivity
ElevenLabs launched ElevenAI, an experimental app for team collaboration, during its 11/11 Summit in New York. The tool, in preview mode, integrates meeting note-taking, voice dictation, and AI agent functionality to replace standalone productivity tools. It offers real-time transcription, cross-meeting data queries, live assistance for recalling past conversations, and dictation across 90 languages with industry-specific terminology support. ElevenAgent enables automated follow-up actions like email drafting. The app mirrors features of Wispr Flow and Granola but adds integration with ElevenLabs’ AI models. TechCrunch noted the preview phase’s unclear capabilities. The launch coincides with Scribe v3 speech-to-text models, which include live transcription, custom model fine-tuning, and language model selection tools. Analysts view the move as part of a trend toward workplace AI as centralized knowledge hubs. ElevenAI’s success hinges on accuracy, integration, and scalability, with early access allowing teams to test workflows. The app aims to reduce administrative tasks by enabling workflow triggers through its agent platform.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: DirectStorage 1.4 uses GPU to cut game loading times with Zstd codec
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Original headline: How DirectStorage 1.4 eliminates game loading times using your GPU
DirectStorage 1.4 uses Zstandard codec to let GPUs decompress game data instead of CPUs, reducing loading times. The technology shifts decompression tasks from the CPU to the GPU, which processes Zstd more efficiently. Users must enable Hardware-accelerated GPU Scheduling in Windows 11 settings under System > Display > Graphics. A benchmark tool on GitHub checks if the system uses this feature, measuring throughput in gigabytes per second. Modern NVMe SSDs should show at least 6-7 GB/s; lower values suggest the SSD is in an M.2 slot connected via the motherboard’s chipset rather than a direct CPU link. Correct installation requires using the motherboard’s manual to locate the proper SSD slot.

item.title: FAA Ends Nationwide Ground Stop After Telecommunications Outage
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica, The Verge, Engadget, TechCrunch, PCMag, Latest from TechRadar US in News, Gizmodo Original headline: FAA Lifts Nationwide Ground Stop After Hours-Long Air Traffic Control Outage
The FAA ended a nationwide ground stop that halted U.S. departures for over four hours on November 13 after resolving a telecommunications outage. The stop, which began at 3:36 pm EST, concluded at 8:15 pm EST. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy cited the FAA’s reliance on outdated analog equipment as the cause, stating that overloaded switches and routers led to inconsistent data, prompting the precautionary ground stop. Over a million travelers were impacted, with thousands of flights delayed or canceled. Air Canada canceled all U.S. flights for the remainder of the evening. The FAA’s website initially faced technical issues but confirmed the ground stop was due to communication problems affecting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers.
item.source: Ars Technica, The Verge, Engadget, TechCrunch, PCMag, Latest from TechRadar US in News, Gizmodo

item.title: Researcher Discovers Windows Zero-Day Allowing System Privilege Escalation
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Original headline: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
Nightmare Eclipse, a researcher with a public dispute with Microsoft, disclosed a Windows zero-day vulnerability named SignDrop. The flaw allows local users to gain System rights by exploiting the Common Log File System (CLFS). Attackers can manipulate Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, leveraging privileged file creation to escalate privileges. The exploit uses Windows Defender's ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature function to trigger the vulnerability. By manipulating symbolic links, attackers force Defender to create files with System privileges, granting access to sensitive operations. The vulnerability stems from a security measure Microsoft introduced in October 2025 to block other CLFS exploits. Nightmare Eclipse noted the irony: "If everything is chained correctly, funnily this legit security mitigation can be used against itself and allow an elevation [of] privileges." The researcher emphasized that Microsoft's implementation, while correct, enables abuse through logical flaws.

item.title: Linux 7.5 adds tool to intentionally crash system via memory errors
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Original headline: Linux is getting a tool that crashes your system on purpose
Linux 7.5 introduces hwpoison-panic, a tool that deliberately triggers memory errors to crash the system. The tool targets kernel-owned pages, allowing developers to simulate unrecoverable memory failures and test kernel panic responses. It supports three page types: rodata (default), slab, or pgtable. By injecting hardware poison errors, the tool verifies that the vm.panic_on_unrecoverable_memory_failure setting correctly initiates a kernel panic. Example usage includes commands like './hwpoison-panic -k slab --yes-panic-my-kernel', which simulates a memory failure at a specific physical address. The tool outputs diagnostic messages such as 'Memory failure: 0x100032: unrecoverable page' followed by a kernel panic. Developers use it primarily for virtual machine testing, recording diagnostic data to confirm kernel behavior during memory errors. Due to its system-crashing nature, it's reserved for specific tests rather than routine use. The tool resides in tools/mm rather than selftests/mm because successful runs destroy the machine, making it unsuitable for continuous integration environments.

item.title: Perplexity Launches AI Agents for Mac App, Expands from Web
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends Original headline: Perplexity Teammates bring autonomous AI agents to the Mac app
Perplexity teammates are AI agents now available on the Mac app, expanding from their web launch. These agents handle tasks like growth campaigns, bug triage, and market analysis autonomously. They plan work, add additional agents as needed, and notify users upon completion. Perplexity notes it’s not the first AI company to offer such agents, citing Meta Muse, ChatGPT Dots, and Grok Bot as competitors. These agents operate on cloud computing, work without constant user input, and communicate with each other via dedicated channels. The feature is exclusive to Perplexity’s Max plan at $200/month, excluding lower-tier subscriptions.

item.title: Nvidia's board considers Arm CEO Rene Haas for CEO role
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: Nvidia board reportedly approached Arm CEO Rene Haas during replacement search
Nvidia's board has approached Arm CEO Rene Haas as a potential successor to Jensen Huang, according to a Financial Times report. Haas is among several candidates under consideration for the CEO role, though no formal offer has been made. The search follows Huang's abrupt departure earlier this week, with CFO Colette Kress serving as interim CEO. Haas, who previously worked at Nvidia for seven years, has experience in consumer and data center CPUs/GPUs, as well as strategic initiatives at Arm, including Compute Subsystems and an AGI CPU. His ties to Huang and Nvidia's board make him an attractive candidate. However, leading Nvidia would require managing a larger organization with a more complex product portfolio than Arm, which has around 10,000 employees. Haas would also face the challenge of replacing Huang, who shaped Nvidia's strategy since its founding in 1993. His potential appointment would create an unusual scenario, as Nvidia previously attempted to acquire Arm in 2020 before abandoning the deal in 2022.

item.title: Philips Launches 100-Inch Ambilight TV with Smart Lighting Sync
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Original headline: The first 100-inch TV with Ambilight is here, and this thing will be super-immersive
Philips has released the first 100-inch Ambilight TV, the The One, featuring Ambiscape technology that syncs with smart lights like Philips Hue, IKEA, and Wiz. The TV replicates on-screen colors with LEDs around the frame and extends lighting to connected devices. It uses a QLED LCD panel with direct LED backlighting, includes four HDMI 2.1 ports, and supports Dolby Atmos and DTS:X. Priced at €2,100 or less in Europe, it is currently available there and in the UK. The One is made by TP Vision in Europe and other regions, while North America uses Skyworth-branded models. Originally listed at €4,300, the TV is now sold for under half that price. Availability in the US and Canada remains pending, with Philips confirming different models exist for those markets.
item.source: Latest from TechRadar US in News

item.title: Scientists Find Most Legal Weed Products Lacking Required Labels
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Original headline: Scientists Bought 480 Legal Weed Products. Most Labels Were Missing Something
Scientists bought 480 legal cannabis products from Colorado dispensaries and found most lacked required labeling. Researchers at the University of Colorado Boulder analyzed the items, revealing only 14% had all mandated information. Flower products were particularly problematic, with half mislabeling THC content. Pre-rolled joints had 60% less THC than advertised. Lead author Grace Macdonald noted compliance with warning labels was 'pretty abysmal.' While 99% of products had the THC symbol and 97% had driving/pregnancy warnings, only 51% included expiration dates. Concentrates had better labeling accuracy, but overall inconsistencies persist. The study, published in August’s Journal of Cannabis Research, highlights risks to public health and consumer trust from unreliable labeling practices.

item.title: Intel Core Ultra 7 260K CPU Listed on Newegg Without Official Confirmation
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: Unannounced Intel Core Ultra 7 260K CPU surfaces in Newegg prebuilt gaming PCs
Intel's Core Ultra 7 260K CPU appears in Newegg's prebuilt gaming PCs without official confirmation from the company. The processor is a downclocked variant of the Core Ultra 7 265K, part of the Arrow Lake family, not the Arrow Lake Refresh line. It features 20 cores, 8 P-cores, a 5.4 GHz boost clock, 125W TDP, 30 MB L3 cache, and DDR5-6400 support. The chip is exclusive to Newegg's ABS prebuilts, including the Kaze II with an RTX 5060 and the Flux II Aqua with an RTX 5070. Intel has not officially released the 260K, and its specifications are based on images from Newegg listings. The model is labeled as U7-260KF in Newegg's option selector, indicating unlocked overclocking but no integrated graphics. The 260K lacks hardware enhancements and the Intel Binary Optimization Tool available in Arrow Lake Refresh processors. Newegg offers the Flux II Aqua at a discount, but Intel has not provided further details on the chip.

item.title: Samsung Adds Birthday Management and Digital Gifts in Contacts App
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Original headline: A new Samsung feature means you'll never forget important birthdays again
Samsung is developing a birthday management feature for its Contacts app, set to launch in One UI 9.5. The tool will categorize birthdays into Past, Today, and Upcoming sections and notify users of upcoming events. Android Authority's APK teardown revealed code for this functionality, which builds on existing manual birthday entry. The update also includes a toggle allowing contacts to share their birthdays with others, visible in contact details. Additionally, Samsung plans to introduce digital birthday cards and gifts via the Contacts app, leveraging its Now Brief feature for AI-generated cards. The tools aim to simplify tracking and celebrating birthdays, reducing the risk of missed events. The features will be available on Samsung phones with One UI 9.5 and later updates.

item.title: Slate Auto Offers Road Atlas as GPS Alternative
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Original headline: Screenless GPS: Slate Auto says, "Remember the road atlas"
Slate Auto's electric truck omits an embedded infotainment system, relying instead on a physical road atlas for navigation. The vehicle, priced under $25,000, features a digital dashboard displaying speed, range, and a backup camera in reverse. It includes two USB-C ports for charging but no connectivity. Slate argues that traditional maps, like spiral-bound road atlases, are sufficient for navigation, citing nostalgia and reduced tech reliance. The company sent a standalone atlas unit for review despite not having a completed vehicle. 'We believe you should use the devices you know and love,' Slate stated, positioning the atlas as a modern alternative to screen-based GPS systems.

item.title: Secretlab Opens US Retail Stores, Launches LA Location and Best Buy Spaces
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: Popular gaming chair and desk maker Secretlab launches dedicated US brick-and-mortar locations — new shop in LA, spaces in Best Buy
Secretlab, known for gaming chairs and desks, is opening US retail stores on November 18. A dedicated location will open in West Hollywood, LA, at 8464 Melrose Avenue, featuring product showcases, consultations, and a giveaway for the first 50 visitors to win a Magnus Evo desk. The LA store will also display special editions like the Pokémon collaboration. Additionally, 15 dedicated retail spaces will debut at Best Buy locations across California, Florida, Colorado, Virginia, Washington, Idaho, Alabama, Pennsylvania, and Texas. These stores will allow hands-on product testing and immediate purchases. Secretlab will stock items for same-day take-home availability. The company recently launched its first task chair, the Atlas, for office use, alongside existing gaming chairs like the Titan Evo and desks such as the Magnus Pro and Magnus Evo.

item.title: Startup Uses Ocean Heat to Power Floating Data Centers
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Original headline: This young startup wants to power floating data centers with the ocean’s heat, and investors are already on board
Drogue, a new startup, aims to power floating data centers using ocean heat. Founder Sam Sipe explained that the ocean holds vast energy, with global warming increasing its thermal capacity. The company’s system, based on ocean thermal energy conversion (OTEC), uses temperature differences between surface and deep waters to generate electricity. A prototype, set for deployment in early 2028, will be installed on a ship, with future versions resembling offshore platforms. Drogue has raised $20 million from investors like Toyota Ventures and XYZ Venture Capital. The technology, tested in the 1980s but abandoned due to cost, now benefits from modern manufacturing advances. Sipe emphasized that data centers are ideal for this setup due to their compact size and low shipping costs. The American Bureau of Shipping has granted preliminary approval for the project. Unlike Elon Musk’s orbital data centers, Drogue’s solution relies on existing maritime infrastructure, avoiding the need for rocket launches.

item.title: FCC Approves 36 Starlink Gateways for Gigabit Speeds
item.description:
Source: PCMag Original headline: FCC Green-Lights 36 Next-Gen Starlink Gateways for Gigabit Speeds
The FCC has approved SpaceX to operate 36 next-gen gateway stations for Starlink's gigabit-speed broadband service. Licenses were granted for stations in California, Colorado, Missouri, Texas, and Washington. These ground-based stations, connected to fiber networks, will transmit data between SpaceX’s satellites and users. The next-gen gateways, using 40 antennas, aim to deliver low-latency broadband and fiber-like capacity. SpaceX’s V3 satellites, with 26 currently in orbit and 26 set to launch Friday, are central to achieving gigabit speeds. SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said hundreds of V3 satellites will be needed by mid-next year for widespread impact. The V5 and Mini 2 dish models are compatible with V3 satellites. Iridium initially opposed the licenses over interference concerns but withdrew its objections, citing achievable coordination. The FCC confirmed SpaceX met interference requirements under 25.203(k).

item.title: Polar Vortex Disruption Sets 68-Year Record, Sparks Early Winter Storms
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Original headline: The Polar Vortex Just Broke a 68-Year Record—and We May Pay the Price at Thanksgiving
The polar vortex reversed direction on November 11, marking the earliest recorded major sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) event since 1958. This disruption sent Arctic air southward, causing record cold temperatures and early snowfall in the Northeast. Meteorologists warn a second wave of cold could hit the U.S. around Thanksgiving. Climatologist Judah Cohen noted the event’s timing complicates forecasting, with models suggesting possible severe storms but uncertainty over severity. The SSW, linked to a strengthening El Niño, is part of a winter shaped by climate change and El Niño’s influence. Andrea Lopez Lang highlighted the unprecedented timing makes historical data insufficient for accurate predictions. Andrej Flis’ analysis of climate models suggests the U.S. East could face Arctic air intrusions and increased snowfall. Cohen emphasized the Thanksgiving forecast remains fluid, with models struggling to predict exact impacts. The early disruption signals a winter of extreme weather driven by El Niño and shifting climate patterns.

item.title: Workday Outage Disables Millions of Employees' HR Access
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: Outage at HR platform Workday locks millions of employees out of their account
A Workday outage on November 13 disrupted HR functions for millions of employees globally. The company placed systems into maintenance mode after discovering an issue during testing that caused inconsistent data, leading to errors when users accessed accounts or completed tasks. Reports spiked at 5:19 PM Eastern time on Downdetector before declining. While it's unclear if all customers were affected, Workday serves 11,500 organizations including Target, Walmart, Netflix, NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, and the US Department of Energy. The company apologized for the disruption and stated it is working to resolve the problem. Employees faced challenges clocking in and out, accessing pay information, requesting time off, and filing benefits during the outage.

item.title: Samsung's Sensor Production May Delay iPhone 18 Launch
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends Original headline: Samsung might be the unexpected reason Apple delayed the iPhone 18
Apple delayed the iPhone 18 launch, possibly due to Samsung's sensor production timeline. Japanese publication Semicon Portal reports Apple may be waiting for Samsung to manufacture enough camera sensors for the standard iPhone 18. Semiconductor journalist Takeshi Hattori links the production delay to Apple’s decision. Samsung began prototyping sensors at its Austin, Texas facility earlier this year, with mass production expected in the fall. Apple has relied on Sony for iPhone camera sensors but is reportedly shifting to Samsung’s Texas facility for new chipmaking technology. Sony acknowledged potential competition but declined to comment on customer-specific plans. The iPhone 18 is expected in early 2027, though the camera production theory remains unconfirmed. Apple hasn’t provided an official reason for the delay, which was initially reported as early as May 2025.

item.title: Apple’s HomeView Smart Display Now Available in Stores
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends Original headline: Apple’s $299 HomeView is finally in stores, with a smarter Siri still in beta
Apple’s HomeView smart display is now available for purchase in the US, UK, Canada, India, Australia, New Zealand, and Singapore. The 7-inch device features a Liquid Retina display, built-in speakers, and the new Siri AI. Two versions are offered: a base model with a speaker stand and a wall-mount variant. Both start at $299, but the wall-mount requires a separate $59.95 USB-C mount or $79.95 wired AC mount. A Power over Ethernet model priced at $129.95 will arrive in early 2027. HomeView can control smart home devices, display security camera feeds, play music, and make FaceTime calls. Facial recognition for up to six users allows personalized messages and reminders. Siri AI, still in beta, has daily usage limits and requires an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad. Potential future features include standalone security camera functionality, though Apple hasn’t confirmed this yet. The European Union is excluded due to Siri AI’s unavailability there.

item.title: Camp Snap Releases Keychain-Sized Camcorder with 720p Video
item.description:
Source: The Verge Original headline: The smallest version of Camp Snap’s retro digital camcorder fits on your keychain
Camp Snap released the CS-8 Micro, a keychain-sized camcorder measuring three inches and weighing 1.5 ounces. It features a tiny LCD screen as a viewfinder but lacks a full display for playback or editing. The device records 720p video with 8x digital zoom and five filters, including vintage effects. It uses a 4GB microSD card for storage, holding 45-60 minutes of footage, and has a 30-45 minute battery life. Priced at $39.99, the Micro is sold in sealed mystery boxes through Camp Snap’s site, Target, and Urban Outfitters starting November 17. Colors like hot pink and lime are more common, while black and glow-in-the-dark variants are rarer. The CS-8 Micro follows earlier models, reducing resolution from 4K to 2.7K on the CS-8 Mini. A correction notes the CS-8 Mini also launches on November 17.

item.title: Physicist's 1960 Prediction Dates to November 13, 2026
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Original headline: It's the end of the world as we know it, per a physicist's 1960 prediction
Microsoft experienced a global outage on November 13, 2026, disrupting Outlook and other services. The date coincides with a 1960 prediction by physicist Heinz von Foerster that overpopulation would reach a breaking point by that day. Von Foerster’s model, like Malthus’s 1798 theory, assumed exponential population growth but failed to account for variables like longer life expectancy and declining child mortality. Scholars criticized his prediction as flawed, noting global population growth peaked in the early 1960s. Mathematical biologist Joel Cohen noted von Foerster accurately captured past trends but missed future shifts. The physicist argued humanity would not starve but would be 'squeezed to death' by resource constraints, a claim dismissed as 'ridiculous' by contemporaries. The outage occurred as the date aligned with the prediction, though population growth has since stabilized.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: Adobe Acrobat guides converting PDFs to Word with online and desktop tools
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends Original headline: How do I convert a PDF to a Word document in 2026?
Adobe Acrobat provides tools to convert PDFs to editable Word documents. The online converter allows quick conversions without installing software, while the desktop application offers advanced features for complex files. Both methods preserve formatting, fonts, and layouts, though scanned PDFs require OCR to recognize text. Free online conversion is available, but desktop features may require a subscription. Users should check converted documents for accuracy, as complex layouts or specialized fonts may need manual adjustments. Adobe Acrobat supports OCR workflows for scanned documents, enabling searchable and editable content. The online converter, as of 11/12/2026, may or may not require sign-in for downloads. For frequent conversions or advanced editing, the desktop application is recommended. The process ensures content remains editable in Word, though results vary based on original document complexity.

item.title: Apple TV 4K users face YouTube app issues
item.description:
Source: The Verge Original headline: The new Apple TV has a YouTube problem
Users of the new Apple TV 4K encountered YouTube app issues upon first use. The YouTube app displayed a black screen with a QR code and error message stating 'YouTube is not yet available on this device.' Some users saw a functional app but with a persistent transparent red bar noting 'YouTube app is approved for device testing only and not for production use.' A software update to tvOS 27.2 and reboot resolved the issue for most, though The Verge’s Tom Warren required uninstalling and reinstalling the app. John Higgins of The Verge called the Apple TV 4K 'one of the best streaming devices available' but noted its higher price compared to other streaming boxes.
